Quant Battle (medium): fixed 120s blitz phase that never ends early, then up to 600s for 4 tactical questions; worst case 12 min per match.
Quant Battle (hard): fixed 120s blitz phase that never ends early, then up to 720s for 4 tactical questions; worst case 14 min per match.
Bot battles (easy, tech/IB): after a wrong or non-perfect submission the player waits for the bot's simulated finish, uniformly 35-85s after match start, with no interaction available.
Bot battles (medium, tech/IB): after a wrong or non-perfect submission the player waits for the bot's simulated finish, uniformly 65-140s after match start, with no interaction available.
Bot battles (hard, tech/IB): after a wrong or non-perfect submission the player waits for the bot's simulated finish, uniformly 100-230s after match start, with no interaction available.
Matchmaking falls back to a bot after 3s, so most battles are likely against bots. battle_started does not record opponent type, so GA4 cannot confirm this.
Mental Math Challenge: fixed 120s round.

data.title: Dead waiting time in bot battles
data.observation: After a wrong or imperfect submission in tech/IB bot battles, the player must wait for the bot's simulated finish (up to ~4 minutes on hard) with nothing to do. Matchmaking falls back to bots after 3s, so this likely affects most battles.
data.hypothesis: Players who finish before the bot leave during the non-interactive wait, lowering battle completion and replay.
data.intervention: When the human has finished, resolve the bot's (already simulated) result immediately and show the result screen. Outcome probabilities are unchanged.
data.causalStatus: untested: supported by code inspection and correlational data only

data.title: Ambiguous answer format in numeric questions
data.observation: Several numeric questions expect a rounded decimal (or a specific unit) without saying so; tolerance-based grading can then reject correct reasoning.
data.hypothesis: Players who get a "wrong" verdict on a correct-but-differently-formatted answer feel cheated and abandon the game or stop trusting the bank.
data.intervention: Show reviewed, clarified wording (explicit unit and rounding) for the flagged questions.
data.causalStatus: untested: supported by code inspection and correlational data only

data.title: Quant Battle is long and its blitz never ends early
data.observation: A Quant Battle is a fixed 120s blitz followed by up to 8-12 minutes for four tactical questions (worst case 10-14 minutes).
data.hypothesis: The match length exceeds what casual visitors budget for, so a share leave before the result screen, especially on mobile.
data.intervention: Test a shorter format (e.g. 60s blitz and a 6-minute tactical cap) once duration data shows how often players run to the limit.
data.causalStatus: untested: supported by code inspection and correlational data only

data.title: IB battles always serve the same three questions
data.observation: Each IB tier has exactly as many questions as a match draws, so every IB match repeats the identical set.
data.hypothesis: Returning players see no novelty in IB battles and stop replaying them; this depresses repeat play for that segment.
data.intervention: Expand IB pools (at least 15 per tier) before any experiment; meanwhile, hide IB battles or label them as a fixed set.
data.causalStatus: untested: supported by code inspection and correlational data only

data.title: Mobile practice submission appears broken or untracked
data.observation: Practice view-to-submit is 2.6% on mobile vs 73.0% on other devices (CI -76.7% to -64.3%). Mobile also has 30.6% engagement and 50 engaged s/user, vs 54.7% and 370 on desktop. Mobile has only 23 users.
data.hypothesis: A mobile-specific defect stops players submitting practice answers, or stops the submit event firing on mobile. Possible causes include a submit control hidden by the on-screen keyboard, a numeric input that rejects decimals or minus signs, or a layout overflow. A gap this large looks more like a defect than a preference.
data.intervention: First, run manual QA of the practice submit flow on iOS and Android browsers and check whether the submit event fires. If a UI defect is confirmed, ship a flagged fix: a sticky submit button and an inputmode that allows decimals and negatives. If the event is not firing, fix the tracking before drawing conclusions.
data.causalStatus: Correlational only. The device gap is measured but its cause is unknown. It could be a UX defect, a tracking defect, or differences in who uses mobile. Nothing is causal until the fix is tested.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 1. It is the largest and most precisely estimated gap in the data, with a narrow CI on a large practice sample. It is likely cheap to diagnose and fix. The impact is capped by the small mobile share, and a tracking artifact is still possible. No allowed experiment metric covers practice submission, so the primary metric is 'none'. Treat this as QA plus a flagged fix rather than an A/B test.

data.title: Battle and question telemetry is too thin or inconsistent to diagnose drop-off
data.observation: No event parameters are registered as GA4 custom dimensions. The battle_started parameter list contradicts the statement that it lacks category, difficulty, opponent type and queue time. Battle and solo funnels rest on 9 and 7 starts with wide CIs. Both new (63.8%) and returning (58.3%) engagement exceed the overall 49.7%, which suggests the segment definitions differ. Most gap metrics cannot yet be measured.
data.hypothesis: The current numbers cannot separate pacing, content and device explanations. Registering the existing parameters and adding a few events would expose where players drop off. The new events needed are opponent_type on battle start and abandon, a question_presented event with question_id, and wait duration.
data.intervention: Register category, difficulty, opponent_type, queue_ms and question_id as GA4 custom dimensions. Confirm which parameters battle_started actually sends. Add opponent_type to game_abandoned. Add a question_presented and answer event with question_id, a correctness flag and time-to-first-input. Add a wait-start and wait-end event for non-interactive phases. Reconcile the new vs returning engagement definitions with the overall rate.
data.causalStatus: Not a behavioural claim. These are known measurement gaps and an apparent inconsistency in the code findings. Fixing them enables later causal tests.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 2. It does not change engagement directly, but it is low-effort configuration and small client changes. Both proposed experiments depend on it: bot_battle_completion needs opponent_type on abandon, and affected_question_solve_rate needs question_id on answers. The evidence that it is needed is direct, from the gap and code findings.

data.title: Forced non-interactive waits in bot battles drive abandonment
data.observation: In tech/IB bot battles, a wrong or non-perfect submission leaves the player waiting with nothing to do until the bot's simulated finish. That finish lands 35-85s after match start on easy, 65-140s on medium and 100-230s on hard. Matchmaking falls back to a bot after 3s, so most battles are likely against bots. Battle start-to-finish is 55.6% (5/9, CI 26.7%-81.1%).
data.hypothesis: Players who have finished answering and face up to minutes of dead time leave before the result screen. This lowers bot battle completion and reduces immediate replays.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, show a 'See result now' control during the post-submission wait. It fast-forwards the bot's simulated finish to the bot's predetermined outcome and goes straight to the result screen.
data.causalStatus: Hypothesis only. The wait is a product fact from code, but no data links wait time to abandonment. Wait time and opponent type are not yet measured, and the battle funnel has 9 starts.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 3. The impact could be high because most battles are probably bot battles. The change is small, local and reversible. The behavioural evidence is weak (tiny n, wide CI, opponent type unconfirmed) and battle traffic is low, so it needs the measurement work. Chosen as the pacing experiment because it is the most targeted pacing change.

data.title: Missing rounding/unit instructions cause correct answers to be marked wrong
data.observation: 11 numeric questions have 3+ decimal answers with no rounding or unit instruction (e.g. qm46, qm47, qm49, qm52). Several have tolerances tight enough that a reasonable lower-precision or other-unit entry would fail. The audit also flags very loose tolerances on 3 questions and duplicate titles on 8. The review below also finds a possible answer/wording inversion (qm79).
data.hypothesis: Some players enter correct answers in a different precision or unit (percent vs decimal, seconds vs minutes, 2 dp vs 4 dp) and are marked wrong. This erodes trust and leads them to abandon or stop practising. Adding an explicit format line would raise solve rates on the affected questions without changing difficulty.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, append a standard format instruction to the 11 flagged questions (e.g. 'Enter as a decimal rounded to 4 places' or 'in minutes'). Answers and tolerances stay unchanged. Questions with suspected wrong answers, such as qm79, are routed to human review separately and excluded from the test.
data.causalStatus: The content defect is a fact from the audit. Its effect on behaviour is unmeasured: per-question solve rate, disputes and abandonment are all gaps. Session-level GA4 data cannot speak to question-level behaviour.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 4. It is very easy (text-only, flagged) and very low risk. It fixes a real defect whatever the test shows. Expected engagement impact is modest because only 11 of 279 questions are affected, and there is no behavioural evidence yet. Chosen as the question-quality experiment because it is the cleanest content change.

data.title: Identical IB battle question sets discourage replay and return
data.observation: IB battle pools hold 3 questions per tier and each match draws 3, so every IB match serves the identical set. Week-1 retention averages 8.4%, and later-day return is approximately 17.9% (20/112).
data.hypothesis: Players who play an IB battle more than once see the same questions every time. Replays become pointless, which suppresses immediate replays and later returns among IB players.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, enlarge the IB battle draw pool using existing reviewed IB practice questions of the same tier (e.g. ibm2-type items) so consecutive matches differ. No new question authoring is needed for a first test.
data.causalStatus: Speculative. The repetition is a product fact. Retention cannot currently be split by category (no custom dimensions), so there is no evidence IB players retain worse.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 5. The defect is certain and fixable with existing content. The affected population (IB battle players) is unknown and probably small, and there is no category-level behavioural data. Revisit once category is a registered dimension.

outline: Add feature flag 'bot_wait_skip' with sticky per-user (or per-guest-id) assignment; attach the variant to analytics events and Sentry tags.
In the tech/IB bot battle client, detect the post-submission waiting state (player done, bot simulated finish time > now).
In treatment, render a 'See result now' button plus a countdown. On click, set the bot finish to the already-determined bot score and transition to the result screen through the existing path.
Verify the bot's score is fixed before the wait starts, so skipping cannot change win/loss. If it is not fixed, compute it at match start in both arms.

Emit wait_started and wait_ended events (with skipped=true/false) for noninteractive_wait_time. Ensure game_abandoned and battle_started carry opponent_type, and register it as a GA4 custom dimension.
Do not change quant battle blitz timing, matchmaking fallback, or human-vs-human battles.
Add feature flag 'question_format_hint' with sticky per-user assignment; attach the variant to analytics and Sentry.
Create a content map from question_id to hint text for the flagged questions. A human reviews the hint wording against each stored answer before launch.
Render the hint under the question text wherever these questions are served (practice bank and battles), only in treatment.

Emit question_presented (question_id, affected=true/false) and answer_submitted (question_id, correct) events. Register question_id as a GA4 custom dimension so affected-question metrics can be computed.
Add a lightweight 'flag this question' control in both arms to start measuring question_dispute_rate.
Exclude questions with a suspected wrong answer (e.g. qm79) from the experiment and route them to content review.

data.question: F-CODE-battle-params lists category, difficulty, opponent_type and queue_ms as battle_started parameters, but also says they are absent. Which is true in the current build? Does game_abandoned carry opponent_type?
Is the 2.6% mobile practice view-to-submit rate a real UX failure or a tracking defect? Does the submit event fire on mobile browsers?
Engagement rate is 63.8% for new and 58.3% for returning users, yet 49.7% overall. Are these computed on different bases (users vs sessions)? Which should be used?
The gap findings list 'missing .' with no detail. Which specific events or parameters are missing for each gap metric?
Where are the quant questions with missing format instructions served: practice bank, battles, or both? Does the answer parser accept fractions or percent signs?
Is the bot's score fixed at match start, or computed at its simulated finish time? This decides whether skip-to-result is outcome-neutral.
Should the fixed 120s Quant Battle blitz phase, which never ends early, be investigated as a separate pacing hypothesis once game_duration_distribution exists?
How many IB battles are played, and how many players play more than one? This sizes the IB pool repetition issue.
Are there any prior experiments, even informal ones, on pacing or question content? prior_experiment_outcomes is empty.

data.observation: Funnel conversion is significantly lower on mobile than on other devices.
data.hypothesis: Input-heavy screens (code editor, numeric entry with live check) are harder on touch keyboards, so mobile players abandon more.
data.intervention: Instrument per-question first-input time on mobile; then test a numeric keypad (inputmode="decimal") and hide code battles on small screens.

data.title: Mobile practice questions almost never lead to a submission
data.observation: Practice question viewed → submitted is 2.6% on mobile vs 73.0% on other devices (difference -70.5%, 95% CI -76.7% to -64.3%). Mobile users also show lower engagement (30.6% vs 54.7% on desktop; 50 vs 370 engaged s/user). Mobile is 23 of 112 users.
data.hypothesis: A mobile-specific defect in the practice answer UI blocks or discourages submission. Candidates are the answer input or submit button being hidden by the on-screen keyboard, or a non-numeric keypad. Alternatively, the submit event does not fire on mobile, which would make this a tracking artefact rather than a behaviour gap. Either way, mobile practice users disengage before attempting.
data.intervention: Step 1: run a manual QA pass on real phones and confirm practice_question_submitted fires on mobile. Step 2: if a UI defect is confirmed, ship the minimal fix behind a mobile-only flag (e.g. inputmode=decimal on the answer field, a sticky or visible submit button) and compare mobile practice view→submit by variant.
data.causalStatus: Correlational only (observational device split). Could be a real UX barrier, a tracking bug, or audience differences. No causal claim until QA plus a flagged fix is tested.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 1. It has the largest and most precisely estimated gap in the data, on the highest-volume funnel. Diagnosis is cheap (QA plus checking event firing), and a fix is small and reversible. Two things temper impact: mobile is a minority of users, and the gap may be a measurement artefact. None of the allowed experiment metrics captures practice submission, so primary_metric is none until practice view→submit by device becomes an experiment metric.

data.title: Forced non-interactive wait for the bot after a wrong/non-perfect submission
data.observation: In tech/IB bot battles, after a wrong or non-perfect submission the player waits with no interaction for the bot's simulated finish: 35-85s (easy), 65-140s (medium) or 100-230s (hard) after match start. Matchmaking falls back to a bot after 3s, so most battles are likely bot battles. The battle started → finished rate is 55.6% (5/9, 95% CI 26.7%-81.1%).
data.hypothesis: Players who finish early and face up to minutes of dead time leave before the result screen. This lowers battle completion and the chance they start another game.
data.intervention: Behind a feature flag, after the player's final submission in a bot battle, offer a 'See result now' action. It fast-forwards the bot's pre-sampled simulated finish and shows the result screen immediately.
data.causalStatus: The wait is a code fact; its effect on behaviour is unmeasured. Battle finish is based on 9 starts and opponent type is not recorded, so the link to abandonment is a hypothesis only.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 2. The friction is certain from code, it likely affects most battles (bot fallback after 3s), and the fix is a small flagged UI change. It ranks below H1 only because the behavioural evidence is very thin (n=9 battle starts) and the share of bot battles is unconfirmed.

data.title: Numeric questions without rounding/unit instructions mark correct answers wrong
data.observation: 11 numeric questions have a 3+ decimal answer but no rounding or unit instruction (e.g. qm46, qm47, qm49, qm52). Their tolerances are tight enough that a common 2-decimal or other-unit entry can fall outside them. The audit reports 0 high-severity issues. GA4 cannot split events by question.
data.hypothesis: Players who answer these questions correctly at a different precision or unit (e.g. 0.57 instead of 0.5714, % instead of decimal, seconds instead of minutes) are marked wrong. This leads to frustration, disputes and abandonment on those questions.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, append a standardised format line to the flagged questions (e.g. 'Enter as a decimal rounded to 4 decimal places' or 'in years, to 2 d.p.'). Answers and tolerances stay unchanged.
data.causalStatus: A content-audit fact with no behavioural data. Session-level GA4 data cannot show question-level behaviour, so any effect on solve or abandon rates is untested.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 3. The change is extremely cheap and reversible, and it removes a clear fairness risk. Expected impact is limited: only 11 of 279 questions are affected, and there is no behavioural evidence yet. It also needs question-level events before results can be read.

data.title: Fixed-length Quant Battle phases make matches long
data.observation: Quant Battle has a fixed 120s blitz phase that never ends early. It is followed by up to 480/600/720s for 4 tactical questions, giving a worst case of 10/12/14 min per match. No match duration is stored, and battle finish is 55.6% (5/9).
data.hypothesis: Players who finish blitz questions early wait out the clock. The long worst-case match length leads some to abandon mid-match or not start another battle.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, end the blitz phase early once the player has answered all available blitz items (or offer a 'Continue' button), leaving the tactical phase unchanged.
data.causalStatus: The phase lengths are a code fact. Actual game durations and where players abandon are unmeasured, so this is a hypothesis without behavioural support.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 4. It is plausible and the change is moderately easy. It is unclear how often players actually finish blitz early. Duration is not recorded and it overlaps with H2, which has a clearer dead-time mechanism, so it should follow H2.

data.title: Every IB battle serves the identical question set
data.observation: Each IB battle pool holds 3 questions per tier and every match draws 3, so every IB match serves the same set. 8 questions also reuse titles across tiers. Week-1 retention averages 8.4% and later-day return is 17.9%.
data.hypothesis: Players who replay IB battles see the exact same questions. This removes novelty and challenge, so they are less likely to start another game or come back.
data.intervention: Behind a flag, expand each IB tier pool (e.g. by adding reviewed questions) so a match draws 3 from a larger set. Measure replay in the IB category.
data.causalStatus: The pool structure is a content fact. Retention figures are site-wide and correlational, and cannot be attributed to IB since events are not split by category. Untested.
data.priorityRationale: Ranked 5. Repetition is certain for anyone who replays IB, but the share of IB traffic is unknown. Writing and reviewing new questions costs more than a UI flag, and retention metrics are noisy at current volumes.

outline: server/index.js startBotMatch: keep the bot resolution in a named function; in the treatment arm call it (and clear the pending timers) from submit_answer once the human has finished.
socket auth: accept anonId in handshake auth; server computes the variant with agent/src/flags/assign.js (same file served to the client as /flags.js).
match_found payload: include { experiment_id, variant } so the client can fire experiment_exposure once.
Default to control whenever the experiment is not live (unapproved, edited after approval, or missing anonId).
server/question-clarifications.js: map of question_id -> reviewed clarification text (drafted by the agent, approved by a human).
Serve clarified descriptions to treatment units in /api/questions and buildTacticalSet; control receives the original text.
question_presented carries { question_id, affected: true|false, variant } so analysis can restrict to affected questions.
Persist /api/flag into a question_flags table so the dispute guardrail is measurable.
